item.title: Part 2: Rationality, Objectivity, and Values in Science
item.description: This article is about part 2 of the anthology Philosophy of Science: Central Issues (1998). This part revolves around the seminal work The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) by Thomas Kuhn, as it proposed radical views on how scientists choose between theories. The debate that followed over the next decades revealed many flaws and inconsistencies on his view of the history of science, and included good arguments about the sources of rationality and objectivity in science.

item.title: Part 1: Science and Pseudoscience
item.description:
This article is about part 1 of the anthology Philosophy of Science: Central Issues (1998).

The question addressed in this part seems simple: What counts as science, and what is mere pseudoscience, blind beliefs, and superstition? At first, we can think of certain criteria that any science needs to satisfy. These “demarcation criteria” have been heavily debated, especially over the last century, and have led to some important realisations in epistemology.

item.title: An Introduction to Philosophy of Science: What is it and Why?
item.description: The word Philosophy is composed of the Greek words for “friend” or “lover” (philo-), and “wisdom” (-sophia). A philosopher is, in a way, someone in a relationship with, and in the process of, attaining ever greater understanding and wisdom. Although one is tempted to think, that wisdom will simply emerge with the accumulation of knowledge, it is only with the awareness of its implications and ethical responsibilities that the philosopher can provide the fertile ground to cultivate wisdom. Reflection upon what has been found, as well as self-reflection on one’s changing intents, thoughts, and interactions with oneself and the world are crucial for practicing philosophy. In this light, we can understand philosophy of science as the process of cultivating wisdom within the philosopher, the scientist, and the practice of science. This is realised not only by studying the methods of the scientific enterprise and their evolution, but also by understanding the consequences that come with the advancements of science, as well as the emerging responsibilities of society.
